title: Determinants of cysteine coverage by chemoproteomics
summary: Covalent chemoproteomics has become a powerful route to expanding the druggable proteome, enabling proteome-wide screening of compounds that covalently modify nucleophilic residues, most commonly cysteine. Yet typical experiments detect only 5-18% of the ~250,000 cysteines encoded by the human proteome, and the determinants of this limited coverage remain poorlydefined. Here we combine cysteine featurisation, explainable machine learning (ML) and robust statistical filtering to establish what governs cysteine detectability in iodoacetamide- desthiobiotin (IA-DTB) chemoproteomics. Using a scalable feature-generation pipeline, we computed physicochemical and structural properties for cysteines and the corresponding tryptic peptides and trained models that predict detectability with high accuracy. Shapley analysis identifies protein abundance and intrinsic peptide properties governing LC-MS behaviour as the dominant determinants, whereas cysteine structural descriptors contribute comparatively little, indicating that detection is constrained downstream of probe reactivity. We further introduce a distance-based statistical filter that improves reproducibility across replicates, and show that cell line selection, subcellular fractionation and alternative electrophiles together expand coverage by >30%. More broadly, this work moves optimisation of chemoproteomics workflows from empirical trial-and-error towards rational, data-driven design.

title: Free-Energy and Molecular Dynamics Analysis of Ser195 and Thr195 Rotameric States in Thrombin
summary: Ser195 is highly conserved as the catalytic nucleophile in trypsin like serine proteases, yet the molecular basis for the strong preference for serine over the chemically similar threonine residue remains unclear. Here, we used well tempered metadynamics and microsecond long molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the conformational energetics of S195 and T195 in thrombin. Well tempered metadynamics revealed distinct rotameric free energy landscapes in both the apo and the ligand bound systems. In the apo state, S195 preferentially occupied a lower angle rotameric state, while T195 exhibited two low energy states with similar free energies. Unbiased simulations further showed greater conformational heterogeneity and increased higher angle sampling for T195. Evaluation of the His57 to residue 195 hydrogen bond further revealed that S195 maintained close hydrogen bond distances across both rotameric regions, whereas T195 exhibited longer and more variable His57 to hydroxyl distances with reduced distance based occupancy. Analysis of the local environment showed that the additional T195 methyl group was associated with redistributed protein contacts. Additional rotamer conditioned analyses demonstrated differences in local packing within corresponding conformational states. Furthermore, solvent accessibility and water contact analyses revealed that the effects of the substitution on the catalytic side chain environment depend on rotameric conformation. Together, these findings demonstrate that two complementary simulation approaches converge on similar conformational preferences and suggest that the S195T substitution alters the rotameric free energy landscape in association with changes in catalytic geometry, local packing, and solvation. These results provide insight into the evolutionary preference for serine over threonine at the catalytic position of thrombin.

title: Mapping the sequence preference of the generalist class II lanthipeptide synthetase ProcM by mRNA display
summary: The biosynthetic machineries of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are often substrate tolerant. A remarkable example is the class II lanthipeptide synthetase ProcM, which naturally functions as a generalist enzyme that has not evolved to use a specific substrate during its evolutionary history. Although ProcM has been studied extensively, the sequence features associated with productive modification remain underexplored. In this study, we use the ultrahigh-throughput mRNA display technique to map the sequence compatibility of ProcM across a focused library. This approach expands the landscape of ProcM reactivity beyond native substrates and individually characterized variants. Machine learning (ML) analysis revealed that the dataset contains sequence patterns associated with ProcM reactivity, with models achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.73. This moderate predictive performance contrasts with the near-perfect accuracy reported for specialized enzymes. This suggests that predicting substrate compatibility for generalist enzymes is more challenging due to uneven representation of reactive and nonreactive sequences and limitations of the available data.. Our results provide a high-throughput view of ProcM reactivity and highlight differences with previous high-throughput studies on substrate selectivity of RiPP modification enzymes. Future studies will need to assess whether these differences are common when comparing generalist with specialist enzymes.

title: Rigidity-Aware Geometric Pretraining for Protein Design and Conformational Ensembles
summary: Generative models have recently advanced de novo protein design by learning the statistical regularities of natural structures. However, current approaches face three key limitations: (1) Existing methods cannot jointly learn protein geometry and design tasks, where pretraining can be a solution; (2) Current pretraining methods mostly rely on local, non-rigid atomic representations for property prediction downstream tasks, limiting global geometric understanding for protein generation tasks; and (3) Existing approaches have yet to effectively model the rich dynamic and conformational information of protein structures. To overcome these issues, we introduce RigidSSL (Rigidity-Aware Self-Supervised Learning}, a geometric pretraining framework that front-loads geometry learning prior to generative finetuning. Phase I (RigidSSL-Perturb) learns geometric priors from 432K structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database with simulated perturbations. Phase II (RigidSSL-MD) refines these representations on 1.3K molecular dynamics trajectories to capture physically realistic transitions. Underpinning both phases is a bi-directional, rigidity-aware flow matching objective that jointly optimizes translational and rotational dynamics to maximize mutual information between conformations. Empirically, RigidSSL variants improve designability by up to 43% while enhancing novelty and diversity in unconditional generation. Furthermore, RigidSSL-Perturb improves the success rate by 5.8% in zero-shot motif scaffolding and RigidSSL-MD captures more biophysically realistic conformational ensembles in G protein-coupled receptor modeling. The code is available at: https://github.com/ZhanghanNi/RigidSSL.git.

title: Impact of the N-glycosylation on full-length IgG2 and IgG4 antibodies: a comparative study using molecular dynamics simulations.
summary: Like other proteins, monoclonal antibodies - important biodrugs- are subject to post translational modifications, especially the N-glycosylations. However, the effect of the N-glycosylations remains poorly studied and atomistic details about their influence are rarely available. . Moreover, the few existing studies focus on the prevalent immunoglobulin G1. To go further in the understanding of the impact of glycosylations, we have carried out a comparative exploration of the effect of N-glycosylations on two different classes of antibodies, namely Mab231, an IgG2 and the pembrolizumab, an IgG4 . The two antibodies differ by their sequences, their length, their 3D structure but also by the location and composition of the glycans. In the present work, detailed and important information were gained through molecular dynamics simulations where both monoclonal antibodies were studied without and with the presence of their glycans. The results of 1.5 microseconds of sampling for each system show that glycosylation does not drastically alter the overall conformational landscape of either antibody, whatever the metrics considered. However, it measurably modulates local flexibility, inter-domain correlated motions, and the relative orientation of the Fab arms with respect to the Fc domain, with statistically significant shifts in key geometric descriptors. Importantly, contact analysis reveals that glycan interactions extend beyond the Fc region to reach Fab residues. The allosteric network calculations demonstrate that the influence of Fc-bound glycans propagates even until the Fab framework regions in both mAbs, which could impact the antigen binding. The nature and magnitude of these effects are subclass-dependent, reflecting differences in glycan composition, hinge architecture, and three-dimensional organization Our findings challenge the prevailing view that Fc glycosylation uniformly promotes CH2 domain opening. More importantly, it underscores the necessity of considering full-length structures and IgG subclass diversity in glyco-engineering strategies.

title: Predicting Lifespan-Extending Compounds Using Supervised Machine Learning
summary: Identifying lifespan-extending compounds is an important objective in ageing research, but experimental screening remains costly and time consuming. This study evaluates supervised machine learning for predicting lifespan-extending compounds in Caenorhabditis elegans using compound-protein interaction features derived from the STITCH database. Three feature representations were compared: continuous interaction probabilities, binary features generated using a fixed threshold of 0.5, and binary features generated using an optimised threshold selected within cross-validation. Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with performance assessed by accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and area under the precision recall curve (AUPRC). Model interpretation was examined using Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI), SHAP, TreeSHAP, and LIME, with Jaccard similarity used to compare the top-ranked protein features. Random Forest achieved its highest accuracy (78.84%), AUROC (0.7391), and AUPRC (0.5202) using the fixed threshold binary representation. XGBoost achieved its highest accuracy (80.36%) using the optimised threshold representation, whereas continuous features yielded its highest AUROC (0.7605) and AUPRC (0.5332). SHAP and TreeSHAP showed the strongest agreement in protein rankings, producing identical top-10 feature sets across all three XGBoost representations. These findings demonstrate that feature representation influences both predictive performance and model interpretation, highlighting the importance of evaluating classification metrics alongside explainability when prioritising candidate compounds for further ageing research.

title: Physics-informed neural network for predicting myocardial mechanics from in vivo physiological measurements
summary: Structural heart diseases (SHDs) are characterized by progressive myocardial remodeling, yet the tissue-level mechanical properties underlying this process cannot be measured directly in vivo. This limitation restricts the ability of conventional physiological measurements to fully characterize myocardial remodeling and disease progression. Here, we present a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that integrates constitutive biomechanics with organ-level physiological measurements to simultaneously infer myocardial biomechanical descriptors and predict physically consistent stress responses. By embedding a hyperelastic constitutive model within the learning process, the framework links physiological measurements with tissue-level mechanics while preserving biomechanical consistency. Using right ventricular remodeling in pulmonary hypertension (PH) as a representative model of SHDs, the proposed framework accurately reproduced nonlinear stress-stretch behavior and outperformed conventional data-driven machine learning approaches for stress prediction. Furthermore, incorporation of PINN-derived tissue-level descriptors with organ-level physiological measurements improved disease stratification and enhanced separation between control, mild, and severe PH remodeling states. These findings support physics-informed constitutive learning as an interpretable framework for integrating organ-level physiology with tissue-level biomechanics and establish a foundation for future biomechanics-informed characterization of myocardial remodeling across SHDs.

title: A synthetic MALDI-TOF MS atlas for microbial classification across hospitals
summary: Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Time-of-Flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry (MS) is central to routine clinical microbiology for species identification. Its combination with machine learning is constrained by fragmented public datasets, species imbalance and acquisition-related variability. Synthetic datasets could provide more training data, but they must preserve the spectral information needed to make predictions on real samples. Here, we present an open, synthetic MALDI-TOF MS atlas comprising 4.3 million spectra across 43 clinically relevant bacterial species. To construct the atlas, we harmonised public repositories from three countries and trained a species- and institution-conditioned concept-bottleneck generative variational autoencoder (CBGM-VAE) on 179,086 measured spectra. We assessed the atlas as both a stand-alone training resource and a complement to real data, using bacterial species classification as a functional benchmark. Evaluation comprised 7,269 real spectra from more than 7 countries, 24 institutions and multiple acquisition platforms, covering: temporal, technical, biological and combined shifts. A neural network trained only on synthetic spectra achieved F1 scores ranging from 0.788 to 1.000 across external cohorts. When synthetic spectra were combined with real training data, classification performance improved or matched using real data only. These findings demonstrate that the atlas retains transferable information and can complement measured data. The openly released atlas provides a reusable resource for supervised learning and benchmarking. It can also be explored for pretraining representation-learning and foundation models in MALDI-TOF MS research.
